name: NoFap / semen retention

lead: NoFap and semen retention are overlapping practices of deliberately avoiding masturbation or ejaculation. NoFap began in 2011 as an online self-help community aimed at quitting pornography and masturbation. In looksmaxxing circles, followers say abstinence brings more confidence, energy and drive, and a more attractive presence.

Proponents propose that retaining semen conserves nutrients or hormones, raises testosterone, or restores dopamine sensitivity, improving mood, skin, jawline or attractiveness. A widely cited 2003 study on testosterone rising after seven days of abstinence was retracted in 2021, and published reviews describe the claimed benefits as unsubstantiated. No published study has demonstrated looks effects.

paras: It involves no product: people set streaks of abstinence, track days in apps or communities, and pair it with exercise, sleep and other self-improvement habits.

Researchers have analyzed distress tied to abstinence and relapse framing in NoFap communities, and a 2024 letter describes a Dhat-like syndrome in anti-masturbation groups. Men's-health content on social media has been rated as largely inaccurate.

angle.text: Followers abstain in the belief it raises testosterone and drive, giving them more confidence and a more attractive presence. The testosterone claim traces to a 2003 study retracted in 2021, and the looks and confidence benefits have not been shown in studies.

lead: NoFap is an online movement and community whose members try to stop pornography use and masturbation, and semen retention is the related practice of deliberately reducing or stopping ejaculation. [1][2] Wikipedia says NoFap was founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread about a 2003 study claiming testosterone rose after seven days of abstinence, a study that was retracted in 2021. [3]

Members cite religious or moral reasons, self-improvement, and physical benefits such as energy, focus and sleep. [3] In looksmaxxing communities the practice is also discussed as a way to improve confidence, social behavior or appearance. [4][5]

Medical authors describe the claimed benefits as lacking evidence. A 2024 study of online ejaculation-training programs found courses promoted with unsubstantiated health claims, and an analysis of TikTok and Instagram found semen retention had the most impressions of the men's-health topics studied, with accuracy rated poor overall. [2][6] Pornography addiction and sex addiction are not recognized as diagnoses in the DSM-5-TR or ICD-11, according to Wikipedia. [3]
infobox: No studies found for appearance benefits

paras: NoFap started as a Reddit community and grew into a forum, positioned as support for people wanting to quit pornography and masturbation. Its scientific claims trace largely to the anti-pornography activist Gary Wilson, whose work a historian has described as pseudoscientific. [3]

Semen retention and NoFap are promoted on social media, and a 2024 study identified eleven online courses teaching ejaculation training, priced from $5 to $147 per week or $20 to $199 one-time. [2] Researchers described a social media environment of highly engaging short-form video in which men consult the internet for sexual health concerns. [7]

Proponents on looksmax.org describe NoFap as a general-purpose solution to confidence problems and frame abstinence as part of the blackpill worldview, while others argue semen retention makes the body more attractive. [4][5] Courses analyzed in 2024 claimed to improve erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, porn addiction, sexual performance anxiety, testosterone levels and depression. [2]
No studies found testing abstinence or semen retention for appearance. The 2003 study that helped spark the movement, which reported higher testosterone after seven days, was retracted in 2021. [3]

Related research includes a 2021 qualitative analysis of NoFap/PornFree forum posts, which found that commitment to abstinence framed as recovery and relapse was a major factor maintaining distress. [1] A 2024 letter describes Dhat syndrome, a semen-loss anxiety syndrome described mainly in South Asia, emerging in the United States from anti-masturbation semen-retention groups. [8] A 2007 study had earlier reported Dhat-like symptoms among white Britons. [9] A 2026 bibliometric analysis mapped 3,239 articles on masturbation, noting contradictory positions between promoting it as healthy and linking it to negative experiences. [10]

Wikipedia reports that psychologist David Ley calls NoFap ideas simplistic and reliant on weak science, and that medical professionals generally attribute members' struggles to other mental health issues. [3] A 2025 narrative review and a 2024 social media analysis both characterize men's-health content online as frequently inaccurate, with physician posts rated more accurate than non-physician posts. [6][7]
On looksmax.org, threads range from posts calling NoFap key to success to posts arguing it has no effect, and members debate whether abstinence is a looksmaxxing tool or a distraction. [4][5][11]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, NoFap and semen retention appear both as endorsed self-improvement practices and as targets of skepticism. [4][5][11]
